display.title: Pre-Sukkos Farbrengen: After Yom Kippur, Now We Do Teshuvah
display.summary_short: Between Yom Kippur and Sukkos: why 'now we do teshuvah' means always growing, with stories of Reb Zusha and the Rebbe, and the parable of the princess for 'Next Year in Yerushalayim'.
display.summary_long: In the four days between Yom Kippur and Sukkos, the storyteller explains how high we reach on Yom Kippur, with five tefillos matching the five levels of the neshamah and Ne'ilah locking us in together with Hashem. Yet when the young Frierdiker Rebbe asked his father, the Rebbe Rashab, what to do after Yom Kippur, he answered, 'Now we do teshuvah.' The Rebbe's explanation follows: we know Hashem forgives us, since we say His name in the brachah of forgiveness, so teshuvah means climbing higher every day. Reb Zusha of Anipoli said he would not be asked why he was not like Avraham or Moshe, only why he was not Zusha. A story told by Rabbi Groner shows the Rebbe asking himself every night, 'Is that all you accomplished today?' Finally, a parable: a princess married to a poor peasant begs her father the king to take her home, because the townspeople honor her only while the king is visiting. So too the Torah, Hashem's princess, cries at the end of Yom Kippur, and we answer, 'Next Year in Yerushalayim': take us to the Beis HaMikdash, where we will treat her as she deserves.
display.lesson: Teshuvah means always going higher, even after Yom Kippur; good is good, but better is better. We ask Hashem to bring the Geulah so we can honor the Torah fully.
